title: Eicosanoids
terms: Signaling molecule made by enzymatic oxidation of arachidonic acid (or similar fatty acids); includes prostaglandins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes.
Fatty acid released from membrane phospholipid/diacylglycerol; the common precursor of all eicosanoids.
Starting substrate at the top of the synthesis pathway; phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from it.
Eicosanoids are very hydrophobic, so they usually act on the same or nearby cells; a few can be endocrine.
First, shared enzyme: releases arachidonic acid. Blocking it (glucocorticoids via annexin A1) cuts off ALL eicosanoid branches.
Converts arachidonic acid to PGH2; drives gastric mucosa cytoprotection and platelet thromboxane A2.
Converts arachidonic acid to PGH2; drives joint inflammation/pain, colon cancer PGE2, endothelial PGI2 (S7 also color-codes kidney and uterus as COX-2).
Converts arachidonic acid to 5-hydroperoxyeicosatetraenoic acid (5-HPETE) → leukotrienes; slide spells it Lipooxygenase-5.
COX-1/COX-2 product; the branch point that becomes prostaglandins, prostacyclins, and thromboxanes.
5-LOX product; precursor of the leukotrienes (slide typo: eicostetraeoic acid).
COX-derived eicosanoid family (prostanoids); e.g. PGE2, PGD2, PGF2α.
Most versatile prostaglandin: gastric cytoprotection, inflammation/pain, colon cancer survival, afferent arteriole dilation in kidney.
COX-2 prostaglandin in joints/soft tissue (inflammation, pain); receptors DP (Gs) and CRTH2 (Gi).
Prostaglandin in joints/soft tissue and in the uterus, where it causes luteolysis.
Endothelial (COX-2) product: keeps platelets resting and dilates vessels via IP receptor/Gs/cAMP.
Platelet (COX-1) product: platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction via TP receptor/Gq/IP3/Ca2+.
5-LOX-derived eicosanoid; LTB4, LTC4, LTD4, LTE4 act in airways and inflammation.
Leukotriene acting on receptors on polymorphonuclear leukocytes (oxidative damage), chief cells (digestive enzymes), and parietal cells (HCl) in the gastric diagram.
Airway leukotrienes (with LTB4): bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion.
Protective, anti-apoptotic eicosanoid effect: COX-1 PGE2/PGI2 in gastric mucosa; COX-2 PGE2 in colon cancer.
Breakdown of the corpus luteum; the uterine PGF2α effect in the functions table.
G protein-coupled receptor; can couple Gs, Gi, Gq, or minor G proteins (G12, G13, Gh).
Seven-transmembrane receptor that activates a heterotrimeric G protein; the receptor type for all eicosanoids.
Main Point: different G protein couplings
Same prostaglandin, different receptor/G protein in different tissues = different effects (e.g. vasoconstriction vs vasodilation).
Gαs activates adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP. Used by EP2, EP4, DP, IP.
Gαi inhibits adenylyl cyclase → ↓ cAMP. Used by EP3, CRTH2.
Gαq activates phospholipase C → DAG + IP3 (↑ Ca2+). Used by EP1, TPβ, FP.
Enzyme that converts ATP to cAMP; activated by Gαs, inhibited by Gαi.
Second messenger made by adenylyl cyclase; activates protein kinase A.
cAMP-activated kinase; mediates platelet resting and smooth muscle relaxation.
Gαq-activated enzyme that produces DAG and IP3.
PLC product and second messenger (slide typo: diacylglyerol).
PLC product that raises cytosolic Ca2+ (slide writes triphosphate).
PGE2 receptor coupled to Gq (↑ IP3, DAG, Ca2+); shown in gastric mucosa cytoprotection.
PGE2 receptor coupled to Gs (↑ cAMP).
PGE2 receptor coupled to Gi/G12 (↓ cAMP).
PGE2 receptor coupled to Gs (↑ cAMP).
Prostacyclin receptor coupled to Gs (↑ cAMP) on platelets and smooth muscle.
Thromboxane A2 receptors; both Gq (+G13, Gh). TPα also Gs (↑ cAMP); TPβ also Gi (↓ cAMP).
PGD2 receptors: DP = Gs (↑ cAMP); CRTH2 = Gi (↓ cAMP).
PGF2α receptors; both Gq (↑ IP3, DAG, Ca2+).
Rubor (vasodilation), tumor (vascular permeability), calor (leukocyte activation/cytokines), dolor (nociception); eicosanoids mediate all four.
Increased pain sensitivity; one of the eicosanoid-mediated inflammatory effects.
Slowly developing lameness, stiffness, pain on flexion, knee swelling, reduced joint space on X-ray.
Stress hormone; synthetic versions are steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that block PLA2 via annexin A1.
Synthetic glucocorticoid; treats inflammation and autoimmune disease but is immune suppressive and catabolic.
Glucocorticoids → annexin A1, which inhibits phospholipase A2 (T-bar on slide), cutting off every eicosanoid branch.
Glucocorticoids break down peripheral tissue (muscle, connective, skin, bone) to release amino acids for liver gluconeogenesis.
Blocks both COX-1 and COX-2; treats pain/inflammation but can cause gastric ulcers.
COX-2 selective inhibitor; treats pain/inflammation without gastric ulcers but can cause adverse cardiovascular events.
Shown inhibiting PTGS1 (COX-1) in platelets, blocking TxA2 production (T-bar on slide).
Gastric diagram: LTB4 receptor on chief cell → ↑ digestive enzymes; on parietal cell → ↑ HCl.
Neutrophil-type cell; LTB4 via leukotriene receptor (LTR) activates it → oxidative damage to gastric mucosa.
Arteriole into the glomerulus; PGE2 dilates it to maintain glomerular perfusion.
Arteriole leaving the glomerulus; angiotensin II raises its resistance to support glomerular pressure.
Tubule cells that sense low NaCl and make PGE2 (PTGS1/2), which stimulates renin exocytosis and dilates the afferent arteriole.
Renin-containing cells; PGE2 stimulates renin exocytosis.
Cascade triggered by macula densa PGE2; raises efferent resistance and Na+/H2O retention.
Filtration rate set by glomerular hydrostatic pressure; NSAIDs can lower it.
Ischemic kidney damage NSAIDs/coxibs may cause in fragile patients.
Hypovolemic, hypotensive, or on RAAS inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers).
traps: Basel: MEMORIZE Gs, Gi, Gq. Gs = adenylyl cyclase ON → cAMP ↑ · Gi = adenylyl cyclase OFF → cAMP ↓ · Gq = phospholipase C → DAG + IP₃ (no cAMP)
Same PGE₂ → EP2 = Gs (↑cAMP) but EP3 = Gi (↓cAMP). TxA₂ → TPβ = Gq. Don't swap EP2/EP3.

COX-1 vs COX-2 home tissues (S7 box colors): gastric mucosa and platelets (TxA2) = COX-1; joints/soft tissue, colon cancer, endothelium (PGI2), kidney, uterus = COX-2; airways = 5-LOX. S28 draws kidney as PTGS1/2. Do not flip platelets and endothelium.
TxA2 vs PGI2: TxA2 (platelets) = aggregation + vasoconstriction via Gq; PGI2 (endothelium) = platelet resting + vasodilation via Gs/cAMP. Opposites.
Where each drug hits: glucocorticoid → phospholipase A2 (via annexin A1, blocks ALL branches incl. leukotrienes); NSAID → COX-1 + COX-2; coxib → COX-2 only. None of the three block 5-LOX directly.
Gs vs Gi on adenylyl cyclase: EP2 → Gs → activates AC → ↑ cAMP; EP3 → Gi → inhibits AC → ↓ cAMP. Same ligand (PGE2), opposite second messenger.
Gq goes to phospholipase C, not adenylyl cyclase: TPβ/EP1/FP → Gq → PLC → DAG + IP3 → Ca2+. Phospholipase C (signaling) vs phospholipase A2 (synthesis) — do not swap.
Adverse effect pairing: 1st-gen NSAID → gastric ulcers; coxib → cardiovascular events; BOTH → AKI risk in fragile patients; glucocorticoid → immune suppression + catabolism.
Kidney arterioles: PGE2 dilates the afferent; angiotensin II constricts the efferent. NSAIDs prevent afferent dilation AND (via ↓ renin) efferent contraction.
Cardinal sign causes: rubor = vasodilation; tumor = vascular permeability; calor = leukocyte activation (cytokines); dolor = nociception. Rubor and tumor are easy to swap.
Same word, different enzyme: "cytoprotection, anti-apoptotic" appears for gastric mucosa (COX-1, PGE2 + PGI2) AND colon cancer (COX-2, PGE2).
Do not memorize the receptor table — but know its Main Point: different G protein couplings explain why one prostaglandin causes different effects in different tissues.

quiz.stem: A horse receives a synthetic glucocorticoid, which reduces eicosanoid production by acting through annexin A1. Which enzyme does this inhibit?
bad: Cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1)
Cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2)
5-Lipoxygenase (5-LOX)
quiz.why: Glucocorticoids act via annexin A1 on phospholipase A2, the first shared step, so arachidonic acid release is blocked.

quiz.stem: Which eicosanoid class is reduced by a synthetic glucocorticoid but NOT by a first-generation non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID)?
bad: Prostacyclins
Thromboxanes
Prostaglandins
quiz.why: Glucocorticoids block phospholipase A2 upstream of every branch; NSAIDs block only COX-1/COX-2, leaving the 5-LOX leukotriene branch intact.

quiz.stem: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) binds the EP3 receptor. Which event follows? (cAMP = cyclic adenosine monophosphate; IP3 = inositol trisphosphate)
quiz.ok: Gαi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP
bad: Gαs activates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP
Gαq activates phospholipase C, raising IP3
Gαi activates phospholipase C, lowering IP3
quiz.why: EP3 recruits Gi; Gαi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP-dependent pathways decrease.

quiz.stem: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) causes different, even opposite, effects in different tissues. Which explanation does the lecture give?
quiz.ok: Its receptors couple to different G proteins
bad: It is converted to different eicosanoids locally
It binds intracellular receptors in some tissues
It is synthesized by different COX isoforms
quiz.why: Main Point of the receptor table: different G protein couplings (e.g. EP2/Gs vs EP3/Gi) explain tissue-specific effects.

quiz.stem: Which tissue – eicosanoid – effect pairing matches the eicosanoid functions table?
bad: Kidney – TxA2 – afferent arteriole dilation
Endothelium – TxA2 – vasodilation
Platelets – PGI2 – platelet aggregation
quiz.why: Uterus PGF2α causes luteolysis; kidney uses PGE2, endothelium PGI2, platelets TxA2.

quiz.stem: A dog on a first-generation non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) develops a gastric ulcer. Loss of which effect best explains it?
quiz.ok: COX-1 PGE2 and PGI2 cytoprotection in mucosa
bad: COX-1 TxA2 vasoconstriction in the gastric mucosa
5-LOX leukotriene mucus secretion in the mucosa
COX-2 PGD2 and PGF2α inflammation in mucosa
quiz.why: Gastric mucosa relies on COX-1-derived PGE2 and PGI2 for cytoprotection; blocking COX-1 removes it.

quiz.stem: A patient taking a COX-2 selective inhibitor (coxib) has a thrombotic cardiovascular event. Which imbalance best explains it?
quiz.ok: Endothelial PGI2 falls while platelet TxA2 continues
bad: Platelet TxA2 falls while endothelial PGI2 continues
Endothelial PGE2 falls while renal PGI2 continues
Platelet leukotrienes rise while endothelial PGI2 continues
quiz.why: Endothelial PGI2 is COX-2 derived and keeps platelets resting; platelet TxA2 is COX-1 derived and unaffected, so aggregation/vasoconstriction dominate.

quiz.stem: Which pairing of a cardinal sign of inflammation and its cause is NOT as stated in lecture?
bad: Tumor – swelling from vascular permeability
Calor – heat from leukocyte activation (cytokines)
Dolor – pain from increased nociception
quiz.why: Rubor is redness due to vasodilation; vascular permeability causes tumor (swelling).

quiz.stem: A hypovolemic dog is given a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and glomerular filtration rate drops. Which change contributes?
quiz.ok: Loss of PGE2-driven afferent arteriole dilation
bad: Loss of PGE2-driven efferent arteriole dilation
Excess TxA2-driven afferent arteriole constriction
Excess angiotensin II-driven afferent arteriole dilation
quiz.why: NSAIDs reduce macula densa and endothelial PGE2, preventing afferent dilation (and, via less renin, efferent contraction).

quiz.stem: Macula densa cells sense low NaCl and produce prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) via PTGS1/2. What does this PGE2 stimulate?
quiz.ok: Renin exocytosis from juxtaglomerular granular cells
bad: Aldosterone release from juxtaglomerular granular cells
Angiotensin II release from macula densa cells
Renin exocytosis from afferent arteriole endothelial cells
quiz.why: Macula densa PGE2 stimulates renin exocytosis from the granular cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

quiz.stem: Which patients does the lecture identify as at increased risk of acute kidney injury (AKI) after non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) treatment? (select all that apply)
ok: A patient on an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor
bad: A patient with osteoarthritis only
A healthy, well-hydrated patient
quiz.why: Most healthy patients are fine; hypovolemic, hypotensive, or angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor/angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) patients are at risk.

quiz.stem: Thromboxane A2 (TxA2) binds the TPβ receptor in the pathway shown in lecture. What happens next? (DAG = diacylglycerol; IP3 = inositol trisphosphate)
quiz.ok: Gαq activates phospholipase C, producing DAG and IP3
bad: Gαs activates adenylyl cyclase, producing cyclic AMP
Gαq inhibits phospholipase C, reducing DAG and IP3
Gαs inhibits phospholipase A2, reducing arachidonic acid
quiz.why: TPβ recruits Gq; Gαq activates phospholipase C to make DAG and IP3, which activate downstream pathways.

quiz.stem: Which statement about how eicosanoids usually signal is correct?
quiz.ok: Hydrophobic, so usually autocrine or paracrine
bad: Hydrophilic, so usually autocrine or paracrine
Hydrophobic, so usually endocrine via plasma
Hydrophilic, so usually endocrine via plasma
quiz.why: Eicosanoids are very hydrophobic, so they are usually autocrine/paracrine; a few can be endocrine.

quiz.stem: A trainer wants a racehorse's osteoarthritis pain treated while avoiding gastric ulcers. Which drug class fits, and which risk remains? (NSAID = non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug)
quiz.ok: Coxib; adverse cardiovascular events remain a risk
bad: First-generation NSAID; cardiovascular events remain a risk
Coxib; gastric ulcers remain the main risk
Glucocorticoid; gastric ulcers remain the main risk
quiz.why: Coxibs target COX-2 only, sparing COX-1 gastric cytoprotection, but can cause adverse cardiovascular events.

quiz.stem: A horse receives long-term synthetic glucocorticoids. Which metabolic side effect is described in lecture?
quiz.ok: Peripheral catabolism releasing amino acids for liver gluconeogenesis
bad: Peripheral anabolism storing amino acids from liver glycogenolysis
Liver catabolism releasing glucose for muscle gluconeogenesis
Bone anabolism consuming amino acids from liver gluconeogenesis
quiz.why: Glucocorticoids are catabolic in muscle, connective tissue, skin, and bone, releasing amino acids that the liver uses for gluconeogenesis.

quiz.stem: A dehydrated dog with arthritis needs pain control. Compare first-generation NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) and coxibs for kidney risk.
quiz.ok: Both carry risk, because renal prostaglandins use COX-1 and COX-2
bad: Only first-generation NSAIDs carry risk, because coxibs spare COX-1
Only coxibs carry risk, because renal prostaglandins use COX-2 only
Neither carries risk, because kidney perfusion depends on angiotensin only
quiz.why: Kidney PGE2 is made by PTGS1/2, and the slide states NSAIDs and coxibs may both cause AKI in fragile patients.

quiz.stem: In the eicosanoid functions table, which pairing of tissue and synthesizing enzyme is correct?
bad: Gastric mucosa – PTGS2 (COX-2)
Airways – PTGS1 (COX-1)
Joints / soft tissue – 5-LOX
quiz.why: Colon cancer PGE2 is COX-2; gastric mucosa is COX-1, airways 5-LOX, joints COX-2.

Checked against slide image: ↓ arterial pressure → ↓ glomerular hydrostatic pressure → ↓ GFR (plus ↑ NaCl reabsorption) → ↓ macula densa NaCl → PGE2 → ↑ renin → ↑ angiotensin II → ↑ efferent resistance (and ↑ aldosterone → ↑ Na+/H2O retention → ↑ arterial pressure); PGE2 also → ↓ afferent resistance.
